_about: Data for the “Can my pet eat this?” checker. status: no = keep away, caution = only with care or small amounts, yes = generally safe, unknown = not checked yet. Each item lists its sources.

aspca_foods: ASPCA: people foods to avoid feeding your pets
akc: AKC: fruits and vegetables dogs can and can’t eat
aspcapro_grapes: ASPCA Pro: grapes, raisins and tartaric acid
purdue_lilies: Purdue vet school: lilies and cats

items.name: Chocolate
items.aka: cocoa, brownies, chocolate cake, hot chocolate
items.dog_note: Theobromine in chocolate builds up in dogs. Dark, baking chocolate and cocoa powder are the most dangerous; white chocolate has very little.
items.cat_note: Cats are affected by theobromine too, though they rarely eat much chocolate.
items.what_to_do: Use the chocolate calculator to see how serious it may be, then call your vet or a pet poison line. Signs often start 6 to 12 hours later.

items.name: Grapes and raisins
items.aka: sultanas, currants, raisin bread, fruit cake, trail mix
items.dog_note: Can cause sudden kidney failure. There is no known safe amount, and size or breed doesn’t predict which dogs react.
items.cat_note: Most reports involve dogs, but the ASPCA advises keeping grapes and raisins away from all pets.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet or a pet poison line straight away, even before any signs appear.

items.name: Xylitol (sugar-free gum and sweets)
items.aka: birch sugar, sugar-free gum, mints, sugar-free candy, some peanut butters, toothpaste, chewable vitamins
items.dog_note: Causes a sudden drop in blood sugar, and liver failure at higher doses. Signs can start within 30 minutes, or 12 to 18 hours later with some gums.
items.cat_note: The Merck Veterinary Manual says dogs are the only pets reported to be poisoned by xylitol. Sugar-free products still have no benefit for cats.
items.what_to_do: For a dog, call your vet or a pet poison line immediately. Keep the packet so you can say how much xylitol it contains.

items.name: Onions, garlic and chives
items.aka: onion powder, garlic powder, gravy, stuffing
items.dog_note: Damage red blood cells and can cause anaemia. Raw, cooked and powdered forms all count.
items.cat_note: Cats are even more sensitive than dogs to onion and garlic.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if your pet has eaten more than a taste, or any amount if it is a cat or a small dog.

items.name: Macadamia nuts
items.dog_note: Can cause weakness, vomiting, shaking and overheating in dogs, usually within 12 hours.
items.cat_note: Poisoning reports involve dogs. Nuts are fatty and best kept away from cats too.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet or a pet poison line, especially if the nuts were chocolate-covered.

items.name: Alcohol
items.dog_note: Pets are much smaller than us, so a small amount can cause vomiting, breathing problems, coma or worse.
items.cat_note: Same risk as for dogs, and cats are smaller still.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet or a pet poison line.

items.name: Coffee, tea and caffeine
items.aka: coffee grounds, energy drinks, caffeine pills, cola
items.dog_note: Caffeine is in the same family as the toxin in chocolate and can cause a racing heart, shaking and seizures.
items.cat_note: Same risk as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet or a pet poison line, especially for grounds, beans or pills.

items.name: Raw bread dough
items.dog_note: Rising dough can swell painfully in the stomach, and the yeast makes alcohol as it ferments.
items.cat_note: Same risk as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet straight away.

items.name: Milk and dairy
items.dog_note: Many adult dogs digest lactose poorly, so milk can cause diarrhoea.
items.cat_note: Most adult cats are lactose intolerant. Milk is not a good drink for cats, despite the old picture.
items.what_to_do: Usually just an upset stomach. Offer water and call your vet if diarrhoea lasts more than a day.

items.name: Avocado
items.dog_note: The stone can block the gut, the skin and leaves contain persin, and the fatty flesh can upset the stomach.
items.cat_note: The ASPCA says birds and rabbits are most at risk from persin. Keep the stone and skin away from cats.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if the stone was swallowed.

items.name: Oranges and citrus
items.dog_note: A few pieces of orange flesh are fine for most dogs. Peel, seeds and stems can irritate the stomach.
items.cat_note: Peel, stems and seeds contain oils that can irritate. Most cats avoid citrus anyway.
items.what_to_do: Usually only an upset stomach. Call your vet if vomiting continues.

items.name: Almonds, walnuts and other nuts
items.dog_note: Nuts are very fatty and can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and possibly pancreatitis. Salted or flavoured nuts are worse.
items.cat_note: Same concerns as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: A few plain nuts are rarely an emergency. Macadamias are the exception: call your vet.

items.name: Raw meat and raw eggs
items.dog_note: Can carry Salmonella and E. coli, which can make pets and people ill.
items.cat_note: Same concerns as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Wash hands and surfaces. Call your vet if your pet becomes unwell.

items.name: Bones
items.aka: chicken bones, rib bones, cooked bones
items.dog_note: Bones can cause choking, and splinters can injure the mouth or gut.
items.cat_note: Same concerns as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if your pet is gagging, drooling, vomiting or straining.

items.name: Salt and salty snacks
items.dog_note: A lot of salt causes thirst and, in large amounts, salt poisoning.
items.cat_note: Same concerns as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if your pet ate a large amount or seems very thirsty, wobbly or sick.

items.name: Coconut
items.dog_note: Small amounts are unlikely to cause serious harm, but the flesh and milk can upset the stomach.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Usually nothing beyond watching for an upset stomach.

items.name: Cherries
items.dog_note: The stones, stems and leaves contain cyanide, and the stones can block the gut.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if your dog ate several cherries with stones.

items.name: Mushrooms
items.dog_note: Plain, washed shop-bought mushrooms are generally fine. Wild mushrooms can be deadly, so never let a dog eat them.
items.what_to_do: If your dog ate a wild mushroom, call your vet now and take a photo or sample of the mushroom.

items.name: Tomatoes
items.dog_note: Ripe tomato flesh is generally safe. The green parts of the plant contain solanine, so keep dogs away from tomato plants.
items.what_to_do: Ripe tomato is not an emergency.

items.name: Apples
items.dog_note: A good treat. Remove the core and seeds first.

items.name: Bananas
items.dog_note: Fine as an occasional treat. They are high in sugar, so keep portions small.

items.name: Blueberries
items.dog_note: A good small treat.

items.name: Carrots
items.dog_note: Low in calories and good to chew. Cut them up for small dogs.

items.name: Cucumber
items.dog_note: Low in calories, so a good treat for dogs watching their weight.

items.name: Watermelon
items.dog_note: Fine without the rind and seeds, which can cause a blockage.

items.name: Strawberries
items.dog_note: Fine in small amounts because of the sugar.

items.name: Green beans and peas
items.dog_note: Fine plain, fresh or frozen. Avoid tinned versions with added salt.

items.name: Pineapple
items.dog_note: A few chunks are fine without the skin and crown. Avoid tinned pineapple in syrup.

items.name: Peaches and pears
items.dog_note: The flesh is fine. Stones and pips contain cyanide and can choke or block the gut, so remove them.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if a whole stone was swallowed.

items.name: Peanut butter
items.dog_note: Check the label first. Some brands contain xylitol (sometimes called birch sugar), which is dangerous for dogs.
items.what_to_do: If the jar lists xylitol, call your vet or a pet poison line now.

items.name: Lilies
items.aka: Easter lily, tiger lily, stargazer, Asiatic lily, daylily, oriental lily
items.dog_note: True lilies and daylilies may upset a dog’s stomach but don’t cause kidney failure in dogs.
items.cat_note: Every part is dangerous, including pollen and vase water. Even a small bite can cause kidney failure.
items.what_to_do: For a cat, go to a vet straight away. Treatment within hours makes the biggest difference.

items.name: Lily of the valley
items.dog_note: Dangerous to both dogs and cats, for different reasons from true lilies: it affects the heart.
items.cat_note: Dangerous to both dogs and cats.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet or a pet poison line now.

items.name: Tulips
items.dog_note: Can cause vomiting, drooling, diarrhoea and low mood. The bulb holds the most toxin.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet, especially if a bulb was chewed.

items.name: Daffodils
items.dog_note: Vomiting, drooling and diarrhoea. Large amounts, especially bulbs, can cause shaking, low blood pressure and heart rhythm problems.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet or a pet poison line.

items.name: Sago palm
items.dog_note: Can cause liver failure and bleeding problems, and can be fatal. Seeds are especially dangerous.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Go to a vet straight away.

items.name: Pothos (devil’s ivy)
items.dog_note: Calcium oxalate crystals cause intense mouth burning, drooling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Rinse the mouth gently with water and call your vet.

items.name: Aloe vera
items.dog_note: The outer leaf can cause vomiting, tiredness and loose stools. The clear inner gel is considered safe.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Call your vet if vomiting or diarrhoea continue.

items.name: Poinsettia
items.dog_note: The sap irritates the mouth and stomach and may cause vomiting. It is less dangerous than its reputation.
items.cat_note: Same as for dogs.
items.what_to_do: Usually mild. Call your vet if vomiting continues.

items.name: Spider plant
items.dog_note: Listed as non-toxic to dogs by the ASPCA.
items.cat_note: Listed as non-toxic to cats by the ASPCA, though cats love to chew it.

items.name: Boston fern
items.dog_note: Listed as non-toxic to dogs by the ASPCA.
items.cat_note: Listed as non-toxic to cats by the ASPCA.
